title: Late Roman Anatolia
subtitle: 330–632 AD · Constantinople's Hinterland, the Cappadocian Fathers, Justinian and the Persian War

categories.label: Power
categories.subtitle: The emperors who ruled from the Bosphorus, the Isaurian rise, Justinian and Theodora and Heraclius's war

entries.label: Constantius II and Julian
entries.hint: Constantine's son Constantius II ruled the East from Constantinople and Antioch for two decades, building up the new capital's senate and population. His cousin Julian, proclaimed in Gaul in 360, took the throne in 361 and tried to revive the old cults in a short reign, passing through Pessinus and Ancyra on his way east, and dying on his Persian expedition in 363.
entries.note: Ammianus Marcellinus 14–25; Julian, Letters; Gregory of Nazianzus, Orations 4–5.

entries.label: Valens
entries.hint: Valens, made co-emperor by his brother Valentinian, held the East from Constantinople. He put down Procopius's revolt, fought the Goths on the Danube, built the great aqueduct of the capital, and persecuted opponents of Arianism. He died in battle at Adrianople in 378.
entries.note: Ammianus Marcellinus 26–31; Socrates, Church History 4.

entries.label: Theodosius I and his sons
entries.hint: Theodosius I, made emperor in the East in 379, made Nicene Christianity the state religion and the capital his home. His son Arcadius and grandson Theodosius II ruled from Constantinople under the influence of palace eunuchs, prefects and empresses, and built the Theodosian Walls. Anatolia was the secure hinterland of the Theodosian court.
entries.note: Socrates and Sozomen, Church Histories; Zosimus 4–5; Kenneth Holum, Theodosian Empresses (1982).

entries.label: Zeno and the Isaurians
entries.hint: Zeno, an Isaurian chieftain from the Taurus mountains, was brought to the capital as a military leader, married the emperor Leo's daughter and became emperor. His rule rested on Isaurian troops and officials, resented by the capital's Greeks. He was driven out in 475–476 by Basiliscus and returned.
entries.note: Malchus; John Malalas 15; Procopius, Wars 3.9; Brian Croke on Zeno.

entries.label: Anastasius I
entries.hint: Anastasius, a palace official who married Zeno's widow, put down the Isaurian revolt, reformed the coinage in 498 and left the treasury full when he died. His support for the Monophysites led to disputes with the Chalcedonian capital. He brought the Isaurians under control and reorganised the tax system.
entries.note: Evagrius 3; John Lydus, De magistratibus 3; Marcellinus Comes.

entries.label: Justinian and Theodora
entries.hint: Justinian, a Balkan peasant's son who rose with his uncle Justin, ruled with Theodora, a former actress and his co-ruler, and set out to restore the empire: the Corpus Iuris, Hagia Sophia, the reconquest of North Africa and Italy and the great fortifications. His Anatolian provinces paid for the wars and for the buildings.
entries.note: Procopius, Wars, Buildings and Secret History; Averil Cameron, Procopius and the Sixth Century (1985).

entries.label: Heraclius
entries.hint: Heraclius, son of the exarch of Africa, overthrew the tyrant Phocas in 610 with a naval expedition. He inherited a war that the Persians were winning and by 622 had trained a new army in Anatolia, which in six years of campaigns reversed the war. The Persian peace in 628 was followed within a decade by the Arab invasion.
entries.note: Chronicon Paschale; Theophanes, Chronicle AM 6101–6121; Walter Kaegi, Heraclius (2003).

categories.label: Conflict
categories.subtitle: Procopius's revolt, Tribigild in Phrygia, the Isaurian war, the Nika riot, Chosroes in Cappadocia and the Persians at the Bosphorus

entries.label: Procopius's revolt
entries.hint: A relative of Julian proclaimed himself emperor at Constantinople in September 365 when Valens was away and held Bithynia and the Hellespont for a time. Valens defeated him at Thyatira and again at Nacolia in Phrygia in 366, when Procopius's own generals went over, and had him executed.
entries.note: Ammianus Marcellinus 26.5–10; Zosimus 4.4–8.

entries.label: Tribigild's revolt
entries.hint: Tribigild, a Gothic officer who commanded troops settled in Phrygia, rose when he was refused the honours he thought due and plundered Phrygia, Lydia, Pisidia and Pamphylia. His demand for the head of the eunuch Eutropius brought down the all-powerful chamberlain and made Gainas master of the court for a time.
entries.note: Zosimus 5.13–18; Synesius, De providentia; Alan Cameron and Jacqueline Long, Barbarians and Politics at the Court of Arcadius (1993).

entries.label: The Isaurian war
entries.hint: When Zeno died, his brother Longinus was passed over for Anastasius, and the Isaurians rose with the support of ex-officials. They were beaten at Cotyaeum in 492 or 493 by John the Scythian and John the Hunchback, and besieged in their mountain strongholds until the leaders were taken and executed in 497, and many of the Isaurians were moved to Thrace.
entries.note: Theophanes AM 5985–5990; John of Antioch; Evagrius 3.35; Malalas 16.

entries.label: The Nika riot
entries.hint: In January 532 the circus factions of the Blues and Greens joined to riot against Justinian's taxes and officials, burning the city centre and proclaiming Hypatius emperor. The emperor was ready to flee; Theodora's speech is said to have steadied him. Belisarius and Mundus's troops slaughtered tens of thousands in the Hippodrome.
entries.note: Procopius, Wars 1.24; Malalas 18.71; Chronicon Paschale.

entries.label: Chosroes I in Cappadocia
entries.hint: In 575 Chosroes I raided across the Euphrates into Armenia and Cappadocia, took and burned Sebasteia and Caesarea, and was defeated near Melitene by the Roman general Justinian. The Persians' retreat across the Euphrates, after a rout, was a rare Roman success.
entries.note: Evagrius 5.9–14; Menander Protector fr. 18; Theophylact Simocatta 3.

entries.label: The Persians on the Bosphorus
entries.hint: In the great war that began in 603, Persian armies took Caesarea in 611, crossed the Taurus, took Cilicia and reached Chalcedon, opposite Constantinople, in 615 or soon after. Anatolia was held by the Persians for several years and their camp at Chalcedon was in sight of the capital. In 626 they joined the Avars in the siege of Constantinople.
entries.note: Chronicon Paschale; Sebeos; Theophanes AM 6103–6118; James Howard-Johnston, Witnesses to a World Crisis (2010).

entries.label: Heraclius's Anatolian campaign
entries.hint: Heraclius mustered his new army at Caesarea in Cappadocia in the spring of 622, trained it through the summer and defeated Shahrbaraz in Pontus and Cilicia before taking the war into Armenia and Persia in the next six years. It was the first Roman offensive of the war and secured the recovery of Anatolia.
entries.note: Theophanes AM 6113–6114; George of Pisidia, Heraclias; Kaegi, Heraclius (2003).

entries.label: The siege of Constantinople
entries.hint: In summer 626 an Avar army and its Slav allies besieged the Theodosian walls while the Persians sat across the Bosphorus; Constantinople's fleet prevented the two from joining, and the siege failed. The city ascribed its deliverance to the Virgin and sang the Akathist hymn in thanks.
entries.note: Chronicon Paschale 1.716–726; Theodore Syncellus, Homily on the Siege; George of Pisidia, Bellum Avaricum.

categories.label: Order
categories.subtitle: The Theodosian Code, Justinian's Corpus, the reform of the Anatolian provinces, the follis and Julian's school law

entries.label: Julian's school law
entries.hint: Julian ruled that teachers must have the approval of their city councils and be morally fit, and that Christians could not teach classical literature, whose gods they did not worship. The measure closed the schools to Christian teachers; Ammianus called it harsh and Gregory of Nazianzus denounced it. It lapsed with his death.
entries.note: Julian, Letter 36 (Bidez-Cumont 61c); Codex Theodosianus 13.3.5; Ammianus 22.10.7.

entries.label: Cunctos populos and the council of 381
entries.hint: In 380 Theodosius decreed that all subject peoples should follow the faith of Peter and the bishops of Rome and Alexandria, making Nicene Christianity the religion of the empire. In 381 the council at Constantinople confirmed the creed and condemned the opposing views. The Church and the state were now one body.
entries.note: Codex Theodosianus 16.1.2; Socrates 5.8; Council of Constantinople canons.

entries.label: The Theodosian Code
entries.hint: Theodosius II had sixteen books of imperial constitutions from Constantine on compiled by a commission of lawyers, published in Constantinople in 438. It is the first general code of the empire and the source of the law of the Western kingdoms. It also shows the imperial regulation of religion, trade and the provinces.
entries.note: Codex Theodosianus, ed. Mommsen and Meyer (1905); Jill Harries, Law and Empire in Late Antiquity (1999).

entries.label: Anastasius's follis
entries.hint: In 498 Anastasius introduced a large bronze coin with a letter M for 40 nummi, the follis, as the standard of the daily market, and ended the hold of the old base coins. A stable small coinage and tax reform, which abolished the chrysargyron, left a full treasury at his death.
entries.note: Marcellinus Comes, Chronicle s.a. 498; Philip Grierson, Byzantine Coinage (1982); Procopius, Anecdota 19.7.

entries.label: The Corpus of Justinian
entries.hint: Justinian's commissioner Tribonian led a team that in six years condensed centuries of Roman law into the Code, the Digest (fifty books of juristic opinion) and the Institutes, with later Novels. The Corpus Iuris Civilis became the foundation of European civil law.
entries.note: Corpus Iuris Civilis; Tony Honoré, Tribonian (1978).

entries.label: Justinian's reform of the Anatolian provinces
entries.hint: In a series of Novels Justinian united the civil and military powers in the provinces of Anatolia — Pisidia, Lycaonia, Helenopontus, Cappadocia — under governors with the title of praetor or moderator, and abolished the offices that had held them apart. The plan was to stop the oppression of the provinces by officials and soldiers.
entries.note: Justinian, Novels 24–31 (535–536); John Lydus, De magistratibus 3.

categories.label: Belief
categories.subtitle: The Cappadocian Fathers, Basil's monks, the councils of Constantinople, Ephesus and Chalcedon, Julian's revival and Theodore of Sykeon

entries.label: Basil's monks and the Basileias
entries.hint: Basil, after travelling to the monks of Egypt and Syria, founded a monastic community at Annisa in Pontus and drew up a Rule for common life, with prayer, work and care for the poor. As bishop of Caesarea he built the Basileias, a hospice and hospital complex on the edge of the city, with doctors and a school.
entries.note: Basil, Letters 2, 94, 150; Great and Short Rules; Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 43.

entries.label: The Cappadocian Fathers
entries.hint: Basil of Caesarea, his brother Gregory of Nyssa and their friend Gregory of Nazianzus, all of Cappadocia, gave the Nicene doctrine its settled form in the language of one substance and three persons. Their work was the basis of the creed of Constantinople in 381. They were educated in the Greek classics and made Greek philosophy an instrument of the church.
entries.note: Basil, On the Holy Spirit; Gregory of Nyssa, Against Eunomius; Gregory of Nazianzus, Theological Orations (380).

entries.label: Julian and the revival of the old cults
entries.hint: Julian restored the temples, reopened the sacrifices and tried to model a pagan church with priests of the Mother, whose cult centre at Pessinus he visited on his march east. His effort to make paganism an organised religion, with his own hymn to the Mother, did not outlive his reign.
entries.note: Julian, Letters 22, 84; Hymn to the Mother of the Gods; Ammianus 22.9–23.3.

entries.label: The council of Ephesus
entries.hint: The council summoned at Ephesus condemned Nestorius, bishop of Constantinople, who had refused the title Theotokos ('God-bearer') for Mary, and upheld Cyril of Alexandria. The meeting was a scandal of rival sessions and mobs in the Church of Mary. It made the city a place of the Virgin.
entries.note: Acts of the Council of Ephesus (Schwartz, ACO 1); Cyril of Alexandria, Letters; Theodoret.

entries.label: Aphrodisias's temple becomes a church
entries.hint: At Aphrodisias, a city of philosophers who clung to the old gods, the temple of Aphrodite was turned into a church by removing the cella walls and building a new nave in the late fifth or sixth century. Statues were defaced and walls inscribed with crosses. The city, renamed Stauropolis, 'City of the Cross', was Christian by 600.
entries.note: Charlotte Roueché, Aphrodisias in Late Antiquity (1989); Kenan Erim excavations.

entries.label: The Seven Sleepers of Ephesus
entries.hint: A legend, current by about 500 and probably from Ephesus, tells of seven youths who fled the persecution of Decius, slept in a cave for 200 years and woke to a Christian city. The legend, which became a cult and pilgrimage site on the Panayırdağ, spread in Syriac and Arabic and entered the Quran.
entries.note: Gregory of Tours, Glory of the Martyrs 95; Jacob of Serugh, Homily; Quran 18:9–26; Ephesus excavations.

entries.label: The council of Chalcedon
entries.hint: Some 500 bishops met at Chalcedon across the Bosphorus from the capital and defined Christ as one person in two natures, which divided the churches of Egypt, Syria and Armenia from those of Constantinople and Rome. The Definition of Chalcedon became the touchstone of orthodoxy for the Byzantine church.
entries.note: Acts of the Council of Chalcedon (Schwartz, ACO 2); Leo's Tome.

entries.label: Theodore of Sykeon
entries.hint: Theodore, a boy from a village inn in Galatia, became a holy man famed for healing and exorcism, was made bishop of Anastasiopolis and travelled to Constantinople. His Life, written by a disciple, is the best account of village religion, miracle and the countryside of sixth-century Anatolia.
entries.note: Life of Theodore of Sykeon (George of Sykeon), ed. Festugière (1970); Elizabeth Dawes and Norman Baynes, Three Byzantine Saints (1948).

categories.label: Expression
categories.subtitle: Hagia Sophia, Saint Polyeuktos, the hymns of Romanos and the poems of Gregory

entries.label: Gregory of Nazianzus's poems
entries.hint: In retirement at Arianzus in Cappadocia, the former bishop of Constantinople wrote a large body of verse in classical metres: autobiographical poems, laments and epigrams, and doctrine. He wrote, he said, to give Christians poetry of their own as a protection against the pagan classics.
entries.note: Gregory of Nazianzus, Carmina (PG 37–38), esp. De vita sua.

entries.label: The early rock churches of Cappadocia
entries.hint: In the volcanic tuff of Cappadocia, hermits and monks began, from about the fifth century, to cut churches, chapels and monastic cells into the cones and cliffs, some with painted crosses and saints. Most of the famous painted churches come from the ninth to eleventh centuries, but the habit of cutting dwellings in the rock began in late antiquity.
entries.note: Lyn Rodley, Cave Monasteries of Byzantine Cappadocia (1985); Robert Ousterhout, Visual Cultures of Cappadocia.

entries.label: Saint Polyeuktos
entries.hint: Anicia Juliana, descendant of emperors, built a domed church of Saint Polyeuktos which Justinian later outdid in Hagia Sophia, with a long Greek poem on its walls claiming to outshine Solomon's temple. Its carved capitals and niches were found at Saraçhane in 1960 and some re-used in Venice.
entries.note: Greek Anthology 1.10; Martin Harrison, A Temple for Byzantium (1989).

entries.label: Romanos the Melodist
entries.hint: Romanos, a Syrian deacon who came to Constantinople under Anastasius, composed kontakia, verse sermons of some twenty-four stanzas with a refrain, sung in the church. The best, on the Nativity and the Last Judgment, are dramatic dialogues. About sixty survive and made him the great poet of Greek hymnody.
entries.note: Romanos the Melodist, Kontakia (ed. Maas and Trypanis, 1963–70); Kontakion on the Nativity.

entries.label: Hagia Sophia
entries.hint: After the Nika riot destroyed the earlier church, Justinian had the architects Anthemius of Tralles and Isidore of Miletus build the Great Church in five years, with a vast central dome on four pendentives, 31 metres across and 55 high, lit by a ring of windows. Justinian said, according to tradition, that he had surpassed Solomon.
entries.note: Procopius, Buildings 1.1; Paul the Silentiary, Ekphrasis (563); Robert Mainstone, Hagia Sophia (1988).

categories.label: Thought
categories.subtitle: Themistius, Gregory of Nyssa, John Lydus, Anthemius of Tralles and John of Ephesus

entries.label: Themistius
entries.hint: Themistius, a philosopher from Paphlagonia and orator, was the spokesman of the Constantinopolitan senate under five emperors. His speeches on kingship and to Jovian and Valens argued that the ruler should be philanthropic and tolerant of religious difference, since God wills diversity in worship.
entries.note: Themistius, Orations 5, 6, 8, 34; John Vanderspoel, Themistius and the Imperial Court (1995).

entries.label: Gregory of Nyssa and Macrina
entries.hint: In the dialogue On the Soul and the Resurrection, Gregory of Nyssa has his dying sister Macrina answer his questions on the soul, God and the body in the manner of Plato's Phaedo. The sister, not the bishop, is the teacher. He also wrote her Life.
entries.note: Gregory of Nyssa, De anima et resurrectione; Vita Macrinae.

entries.label: Eunapius of Sardis
entries.hint: Eunapius, a pagan teacher of rhetoric from Sardis, wrote the Lives of the Philosophers and Sophists, a record of late Neoplatonism in Asia, and a continuation of Dexippus's history. He was an anti-Christian witness to the changing world of Anatolian cities.
entries.note: Eunapius, Lives of the Sophists and fragments of the History; Roger Blockley, The Fragmentary Classicising Historians (1981).

entries.label: Anthemius of Tralles
entries.hint: Anthemius, the architect of Hagia Sophia, was a mathematician who wrote On Remarkable Mechanical Devices, a treatise on burning mirrors and conic sections. His brother Alexander wrote the best medical treatise of the sixth century. The family from Tralles was one of the most gifted of the age.
entries.note: Anthemius, Peri paradoxon mechematon; Alexander of Tralles, Therapeutica; Agathias 5.6.

entries.label: John Lydus of Philadelphia
entries.hint: John Lydus, a Lydian civil servant in the praetorian prefecture, wrote On the Magistracies of the Roman State, a history of the offices of the empire, and a bitter account of the reforms of Justinian's financial minister John the Cappadocian. It is the best insider view of the late Roman bureaucracy.
entries.note: John Lydus, De magistratibus, ed. Bandy (1983).

entries.label: John of Ephesus
entries.hint: John, a Monophysite bishop of Ephesus and missionary to the pagans of Asia, wrote in Syriac a Church History and the Lives of the Eastern Saints, and left the best eyewitness account of the plague of 542 and of persecution by Justinian and his successors.
entries.note: John of Ephesus, Lives of the Eastern Saints; Ecclesiastical History; Susan Ashbrook Harvey, Asceticism and Society in Crisis (1990).

categories.label: Economy
categories.subtitle: The oil and ware of the late-antique boom and the treasure of Anastasius

entries.label: The late antique boom of the countryside
entries.hint: From the fifth century to the sixth, rural settlement in Lycia, Pisidia, Cilicia and Cappadocia reached its peak, as is clear from farmsteads, presses for oil and wine, and a trade in red-slip table ware from Sagalassos and elsewhere. Olive oil and wine fed the capital's market and the army.
entries.note: Marc Waelkens et al., Sagalassos excavation reports; Hansgerd Hellenkemper and Friedrich Hild, Kilikien und Isaurien (1990); Kyaneai survey (Frank Kolb).

entries.label: The treasure of Anastasius
entries.hint: When Anastasius died, Procopius says, he left in the treasury some 320,000 pounds of gold, the fruit of strict economy and tax reform. Justinian spent it, with the revenue of Anatolia and the East, on buildings and wars in the following decades.
entries.note: Procopius, Anecdota 19.7; John Lydus, De magistratibus 3.

categories.label: Technology
categories.subtitle: The dome of Hagia Sophia, the Theodosian Walls and the aqueduct of Valens

entries.label: The aqueduct of Valens
entries.hint: Valens built a great aqueduct to bring water from Thrace to the capital, completed at the end of his reign. Its arcades still straddle the valley between the hills. The cisterns and aqueducts that stored the water were a part of the city's survival strategy.
entries.note: Socrates 4.8; Themistius, Oration 11; Cyril Mango on Constantinople's aqueducts.

entries.label: The Theodosian Walls
entries.hint: The city's land walls, six kilometres across the peninsula, were built in 413 under the prefect Anthemius and rebuilt after the earthquake of 447 in two months by the prefect Constantine, with a double wall, a moat and some ninety-six towers. The land walls were not breached until 1453.
entries.note: Chronicon Paschale s.a. 413, 447; CIL III 734; Brian Croke on the Theodosian walls.

entries.label: The dome of Hagia Sophia
entries.hint: Anthemius and Isidore raised a very shallow dome over a square on four massive piers with pendentives. In 558 an earthquake brought down its eastern part, and Isidore the Younger rebuilt it higher and steeper to the form that stands today. The building shows the late Roman command of brick, mortar and vaulted construction.
entries.note: Procopius, Buildings 1.1; Agathias 5.9; Rowland Mainstone, Hagia Sophia (1988).

categories.label: Exchange
categories.subtitle: The silkworm eggs, the Eternal Peace, the partition of Armenia and Egeria's road

entries.label: Egeria's pilgrimage through Anatolia
entries.hint: A Western nun, Egeria, travelled to the Holy Land and wrote a long letter home on the way, which tells of her route through Bithynia, Galatia and Cappadocia and her stay at the shrine of Saint Thecla at Seleucia. The text shows the roads and the pilgrimage economy of late antique Anatolia.
entries.note: Egeria, Itinerarium (Peregrinatio) 23; John Wilkinson, Egeria's Travels (1999).

entries.label: The partition of Armenia
entries.hint: Theodosius I and Shapur III agreed a partition of Armenia, in which the Romans took the smaller western part and the Persians the larger eastern part, around 387. The line ran along the upper Euphrates and put the Armenian highlands under two crowns.
entries.note: Procopius, Buildings 3.1; Faustus of Byzantium; Nina Garsoïan in Hovannisian, Armenian People vol. 1.

entries.label: The Eternal Peace and the Fifty Years' Peace
entries.hint: In 532, to free his army for the West, Justinian bought the Persians' peace for 11,000 pounds of gold, which was called the Eternal Peace and lasted eight years. In 562 a fifty-year peace, with a yearly payment of 30,000 solidi and clauses on trade, religion and the Caucasus, was agreed.
entries.note: Procopius, Wars 1.22; Menander Protector fr. 6 (the treaty of 562).

entries.label: The silkworm eggs
entries.hint: Monks from Serindia are said to have brought silkworm eggs hidden in hollow canes to Justinian in about 552, and so broken Persia's hold on the silk trade. Whatever the exact story, the Byzantine silk industry that began at Constantinople and spread to Syrian and Anatolian cities dates from Justinian's age.
entries.note: Procopius, Wars 8.17; Theophanes of Byzantium, FHG 4.270; Anna Muthesius, Byzantine Silk Weaving (1995).

categories.label: World
categories.subtitle: The new capital, the plague of Justinian, the earthquakes and the decline of Sagalassos

entries.label: The new capital draws Anatolia
entries.hint: Constantinople, founded in 330, grew into a city of several hundred thousand, with a senate and a grain dole. The demand of the capital reshaped Anatolia: the harbours of the Marmara and the Black Sea, the roads from Nicomedia and Nicaea, and the estates of the senatorial class in Bithynia and Phrygia.
entries.note: Cyril Mango, Le développement urbain de Constantinople (1985); Gilbert Dagron, Naissance d'une capitale (1974).

entries.label: The earthquakes
entries.hint: The earthquake of 24 August 358 destroyed Nicomedia, and the later quakes of 447, 526 and 557 shook Constantinople, Antioch and the cities of the East. Their cost in buildings and lives — the city rebuilt, tax remitted — is recorded in the chronicles. The Anatolian fault is a constant of its history.
entries.note: Ammianus 17.7; Libanius, Oration 61; Procopius, Buildings; Malalas.

entries.label: The decline of Sagalassos
entries.hint: Sagalassos, a large city in Pisidia with a basilica, library and fountain complex, shows a sharp contraction after about 540: plague, an earthquake, the withdrawal of the elite and, soon, the Persian and Arab wars. By the mid-seventh century it was a village on a hill. Many cities in Anatolia went the same way.
entries.note: Marc Waelkens and Jeroen Poblome (eds), Sagalassos reports (1993–); Mitchell, Anatolia vol. 2.

entries.label: The plague of Justinian
entries.hint: The bubonic plague reached Constantinople from Egypt in 542 and, as Procopius says, killed up to 10,000 people a day at its height. It returned in waves for two centuries. Its effect on the cities and the countryside of Anatolia was serious.
entries.note: Procopius, Wars 2.22–23; John of Ephesus (in Pseudo-Dionysius); Lester Little (ed.), Plague and the End of Antiquity (2007).

categories.label: Lives
categories.subtitle: Macrina, Theodora, Eutropius, Olympias and the law on 'acts against nature'

entries.label: Macrina the Younger
entries.hint: Macrina, the elder sister of Basil and Gregory of Nyssa, made her family estate on the Iris river into a religious community of women and slaves who lived as equals, and taught her brothers. Gregory's Life of her and his dialogue with her on her deathbed show a woman as a spiritual authority.
entries.note: Gregory of Nyssa, Life of Macrina; De anima et resurrectione; Anna Silvas, Macrina the Younger (2008).

entries.label: Olympias the deaconess
entries.hint: Olympias, a wealthy young widow of Constantinople, gave her fortune to the church and the poor and became a deaconess and the friend and supporter of John Chrysostom. She kept a convent of about fifty women near Hagia Sophia and died in exile at Nicomedia.
entries.note: Palladius, Dialogue on the Life of John Chrysostom; Life of Olympias; Elizabeth Clark, Jerome, Chrysostom and Friends (1979).

entries.label: Eutropius the eunuch
entries.hint: A slave who was castrated as a boy and rose to be grand chamberlain, Eutropius became in 399 the first eunuch to be consul and a patrician. He was attacked by Claudian and Synesius and, when he lost Gainas's and the empress's favour, he was dragged from the altar of Hagia Sophia and exiled and executed.
entries.note: Claudian, In Eutropium; Zosimus 5.8–18; Synesius, De regno; Kathryn Ringrose, The Perfect Servant (2003).

entries.label: Theodora
entries.hint: Theodora, daughter of a bear-keeper of the Hippodrome and actress in her youth, married Justinian after a law of Justin I made marriage to a former actress possible. As empress she took part in government, received ambassadors and carried laws against forced prostitution. In the Nika riot she is said to have urged him to stand.
entries.note: Procopius, Anecdota 9–10; Procopius, Wars 1.24; John of Ephesus; Averil Cameron 1985.

entries.label: Justinian's laws on acts 'against nature'
entries.hint: Justinian's Novel 77 (538), against blasphemy and sexual acts between men, said that such acts had brought famine, earthquakes and plague, and ordered punishment with torture and mutilation; Novel 141 (559) offered repentance. The law was written in the aftermath of calamity, as sin that had to be removed to avert divine wrath.
entries.note: Justinian, Novellae 77 and 141; Procopius, Anecdota 11.34–36 (cases against bishops); Dale Martin on late antique sexuality.
